1.tell: Three options (A, B, C) are all COMPATIBLE with a conditional claim ('contact works only under equal status / shared goals / institutional support'); only D denies the necessity of those conditions. When 3 of 4 options can coexist with the claim, the odd one out is the key. D also carries the hedge-word load ('merely lived alongside', 'durably') typical of keys here.

2.tell: Inference template: B/C/D are absolutes ('caused', 'no meaningful effect', 'could not have occurred at all'). A is the only calibrated middle claim ('accelerate without being the decisive cause'). Keys in this bank are the causally hedged option; distractors sit at the two poles plus one reversal.

3.tell: A ('permanently fixed and immune to ANY further change') and B ('most accurately') are superlatives; D is an off-axis anatomical claim the question stem doesn't touch. C is the only modal option ('may diverge more'). Modal verb = key marker in the inference block.

4.tell: Stem says 'the author's ALTERNATIVE explanation' — for wrasse mark tests the standard alternative is 'it's parasite/blemish-cleaning instinct, not self-recognition'. A and C SUPPORT that alternative; B supports it too (wrasses are worse than apes). Only D breaks it: marks resembling nothing they clean. The weaken-item template is 'three options reinforce the target claim, one severs its mechanism'.

5.tell: Cross-text block invariant: the key is the option that shifts the MECHANISM to selection/confounding rather than denying the effect. D is a flat denial, A is a magnitude quibble, C proposes a rival mechanism but concedes the effect is real (too friendly to Text 1 to be a 'respond to' key). B is the sorting/self-selection rebuttal — the standard Text-2 move.

6.tell: 'Would most likely agree' items: B is 'single-handedly', C is a flat failure claim, D is 'primarily... in spite of'. A is the only both/and option ('coincided with AND took advantage of changes already underway'). The key is the option that makes the subject a participant in a larger trend rather than a sole cause.

7.tell: Function-of-phrase item. 'Underground' = hidden, not removed. D is the only option that preserves BOTH halves of the metaphor (power persists + it is concealed). A adds a conspiracy not in the phrase, B inverts the valence to praise, C changes who holds the power. Key = the literal-metaphor-preserving gloss.

8.tell: Structure block: A is a call to action (SAT structure keys are never exhortations), C is factually wrong about equal temperament, D is 'chronological account... corrected one another's errors' (progress narrative). B is the trade-off reframing. Across this whole bank the structure key is the option containing a REVERSAL word — qualification, shortfall, reinterprets, paradox, concedes.

9.tell: Same reversal template: D contains 'revise a heroic narrative'. C is the un-revised heroic narrative intensified ('if anything understated'), A and B are content claims. Purpose keys here rehabilitate the critics/complicate the hero.

10.tell: B is a prescription, C is a popularity history, D is a how-to. Only A describes an argumentative shape at all ('frames a tension... states the paradox'). In this block three distractors describe the wrong GENRE of text and the key is the sole rhetorical-structure description.

11.tell: Textbook concede-then-narrow: 'agreeing that scarcity pushed wages upward BUT adding that the outcome depended on whether legal restraint succeeded'. A is frictionless-market overreach, B claims the Statute succeeded outright, D is flat denial. The two-clause concessive option is the key throughout the cross-text block.

12.tell: Reversal-word test again: 'sets up an expectation... and then reveals a crucial shortfall'. A is a comparison-to-decide, C is a chronicle, D is a no-effect claim. Three-beat structure options beat one-beat ones in this block.

13.tell: 'Would disagree over' items: the key must be a proposition each text actually takes a side on. A (diligence) and D (elections) are things both sides would accept — classic agreement distractors. C is an empirical premise the trustee side asserts and the delegate side needn't deny. B is the delegate/trustee crux itself.

14.tell: B ('has now replaced... overturning') and C ('by themselves', 'entire rock record') are the two poles; D asserts uniformity of RATE, which is precisely the strawman modern geology dropped. A is the synthesis option — catastrophe admitted, known-causes principle retained. Modern-view keys are always the reconciliation, never a victory for either camp.

15.tell: Contains the explicit concessive: 'By conceding a conventional view of the genre before locating its appeal in a different, less obvious function'. C is that conventional view stated flat, B is its opposite, A is a developmental history. 'How the author advances the argument' keys in this bank are always concede-then-relocate.

16.tell: Response items: A ('always'), B ('denies... any particular jobs' — an absurd denial no Text 2 makes), C ('has already caused permanent mass unemployment' — overshoots). D is the this-time-may-differ hedge with a stated reason (cognitive work). Key = qualified doubt, distractors = the two absolutes plus a strawman denial.

17.tell: C is the dependency/presupposition claim; B is its relativist inversion ('no determinate truth'), A is a historical claim about modernity, D requires outside evidence. The 'author would agree' key is the option about what a concept PRESUPPOSES, not what it proves.

18.tell: 'How would Text 2 characterize the proxy' — a proxy under attack. C keeps it useful but inverts which cases it flags (incoherent), D concedes validity and objects on cost (wrong axis: the debate is validity, not budget), A rescues it for a subset. B states the clean validity failure: origin does not track impact. Key = the option attacking the proxy on its own axis.

19.tell: Skeptic about the bilingual advantage = the effect is a publication/small-study artifact. C is a dose-response finding (supports the believers), D shows a real if narrow effect, B is about trainability and irrelevant to whether the advantage exists. A is the only option about the EVIDENCE BASE rather than the phenomenon — the support-the-skeptic key is always the methodological one.

20.tell: Reversal word 'reinterprets... to reach an opposing conclusion'. B is a defense (right direction, wrong shape — and loaded with passage-specific detail, a distractor tell here), A is a sourcing history, D a two-author comparison. Structure keys in this bank are abstract and contain a pivot; detail-stuffed options are decoys.

21.tell: Word-in-context: 'temperate' has three concrete everyday senses (A abstaining, B mild climate, D lukewarm) and one abstract transferred sense (C measured). SAT word-in-context keys are the secondary/abstract sense; the familiar literal senses are the trap. D is also pejorative, which a neutral stem rarely wants. Passage-dependent, so lower confidence.

22.tell: C ('imposes no new costs on anyone') agrees with Text 1 and so cannot be a characterization by an opposing Text 2; D says Text 1 is too cautious (wrong direction); B disputes a factual premise rather than the argument. A is the relocate-not-remove reframing — the standard key shape for 'characterize the argument' items.

23.tell: A is a flat denial of the premise, C is agreement, D is an unrelated counter-proposal. B is the quality-not-quantity condition — the key adds a MODERATOR to Text 1's conclusion rather than rejecting it. Same shape as items 11, 16 and 22.

24.tell: A overshoots ('fails to capture even the diminishment'), B is the naive view being critiqued, D is a motive claim the stem doesn't support. C is the appearance/reality formulation ('presents a constructed viewpoint as if it were an unmediated record') — the 'most strongly supported' key is the critique-stating middle term between the naive claim and its overstated negation.
